framing: Most GPU trouble comes down to three plain questions
paragraphs: The weights fit on your GPU, but training runs out of memory. A forward pass timed at two milliseconds actually takes twenty times longer. The memory bar reads 95 percent while the GPU sits idle. Each surprise can waste an afternoon on a rented machine.
Build a picture of where the numbers live and what the machine does while Python appears to wait. Three questions guide us: will it fit, is the GPU working, and is the measurement real?

Carry a seven-billion-parameter model through a 24 GB budget. Compare FP32, FP16, and BF16, then count everything a training step retains beyond the weights. This arithmetic lets you assess the machine before renting it.
This is our last stop before language. Earlier chapters mostly began with numbers already prepared. Next, sequence length and memory will give us a practical reason to ask what a token is.
outcomes: Estimate a model's memory for serving and for training before you touch a GPU, and explain which step of the loop will run out first.
Tell FP32, FP16, and BF16 apart by what each one gives up, and spot the symptoms of overflow and lost updates.
Time GPU work correctly, and tell a busy GPU from one that is merely full.
question: A model's weights take 14 GB and your GPU has 24 GB. How would you find out whether you can train it, without running anything?
